captions.instagram:
What is the photoelectric effect?

Shine red light on zinc and nothing happens, however bright. Shine a little ultraviolet and electrons fly out at once. Run the experiment that won Einstein his Nobel Prize, find Planck's constant from a straight line, then see the same idea inside night-vision goggles, lift doors, camera sensors and solar panels.

→ Shine light on metal and electrons fly out, but only when each photon carries enough energy.
→ Bluer light gives faster electrons. The stopping voltage climbs in a straight line of slope h over e.
→ A photomultiplier turns one freed electron into millions: four or five more at every dynode.
→ Night-vision goggles do it for a whole picture. Under starlight the grain you see is single photons.
→ A lift door watches an invisible infrared beam. Break it, the current stops, and the door stays open.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/photoelectricclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: What is the photoelectric effect? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Shine red light on zinc and nothing happens, however bright. Shine a little ultraviolet and electrons fly out at once. Run the experiment that won Einstein his Nobel Prize, find Planck's constant from a straight line, then see the same idea inside night-vision goggles, lift doors, camera sensors and solar panels.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/photoelectricclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/photoelectricclear

In this video:
• The experiment. Light on a clean metal plate in a vacuum knocks out electrons.
• Counting photons. A photomultiplier frees one electron per photon caught, then multiplies it 4 or 5 times at each of ten or so dynodes: a gain of millions.
• Light as a switch. Inside a semiconductor a photon frees an electron without throwing it out: the internal photoelectric effect.
• Solar cells and camera pixels. A solar cell uses the related photovoltaic effect: light frees electrons and holes inside silicon and a p–n junction steers them round a circuit.
• Limits and a myth. A wave would need seconds or hours to free an electron in dim light; in fact it takes under 3 billionths of a second.
